title: What Types of HVAC Air Filters Are There?
h1: What Types of HVAC Air Filters Are There, and Which One Should You Use?
description: Compare fiberglass, pleated, electrostatic, media and carbon HVAC filters, learn what MERV ratings mean and how to pick the right filter for your home.
quick_answer: The main HVAC filter types are fiberglass, pleated, electrostatic (washable or disposable), thick media filters and activated carbon filters. Pleated filters rated around MERV 8 to 13 suit most homes. Higher ratings catch finer particles like smoke and pollen, but your system has to be able to move air through them.
body:
Walk down the filter aisle and you'll see dozens of options that look nearly the same. The differences come down to what the filter is made of, how thick it is and how fine a particle it can catch. The right choice depends on your system, your household and what you're trying to keep out of the air.

What are the main types of HVAC filters?

  • Fiberglass filters. These thin, flat filters are cheap and let air through easily. They protect the equipment from large debris but do very little for dust, pollen or pet dander.
  • Pleated filters. Made of folded polyester or cotton paper, pleated filters have more surface area and catch much smaller particles. They are the standard choice for most homes.
  • Electrostatic filters. These use a static charge to attract particles. Some are washable and reusable. Washable versions need regular rinsing and must dry completely before going back in, or they can grow mold.
  • Media filters. These are thick filters, often four or five inches deep, that sit in a dedicated cabinet next to the furnace or air handler. The extra depth gives high filtration with less airflow resistance, and they usually last longer between changes.
  • Activated carbon filters. A carbon layer helps absorb odors from cooking, pets and smoke. Carbon is usually combined with a pleated filter rather than used alone.

True HEPA filtration usually isn't possible in a standard residential system without a separate unit, because the dense material restricts too much airflow for most blowers.

What does the MERV rating mean?

MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It runs from 1 to 16 for most filters you'll find, and a higher number means the filter traps smaller particles.

MERV rangeWhat it catches wellTypical use
1 to 4Lint, large dust, debrisBasic equipment protection
5 to 8Dust, mold spores, larger pollenStandard homes
9 to 12Finer dust, pet dander, most pollenHomes with pets or allergies
13 to 16Fine particles, including much of the smoke in the airAllergies, smoke concerns, if the system can handle it

Some stores use their own rating scales. If the package lists a MERV number, use that to compare.

Is a higher MERV filter always better?

Not always. A denser filter catches more, but it also makes the blower work harder. If your return duct is undersized or the filter is a thin one-inch type, a high-MERV filter can starve the system of air. That can lead to a frozen AC coil, a furnace that overheats and shuts off, or rooms that never get comfortable.

If you want better filtration, a deeper media cabinet is often the better answer than squeezing a dense filter into a thin slot. A technician can measure the system's static pressure and tell you what it can handle.

Which filter makes sense for San Diego and Orange County homes?

Local conditions change the picture a bit:

  • Wildfire smoke. During smoke events, a MERV 13 filter, if your system can handle it, catches far more fine particles than a basic filter. Run the fan to keep air moving through it.
  • Santa Ana winds. Dry, dusty wind loads filters quickly. Check them after a windy stretch.
  • Pets and allergies. A MERV 11 to 13 pleated or media filter helps with dander and pollen.
  • Coastal homes. Damp air and a washable filter that never fully dries can be a bad mix. Disposable pleated filters are simpler.

If filters alone aren't solving the problem, our indoor air quality services include air purifiers, UV lights and humidity control.

How often should you change each type?

Follow the filter maker's instructions, but here are general guidelines:

  • One-inch fiberglass and pleated filters: check monthly, replace every one to three months.
  • Four- or five-inch media filters: often every six to twelve months.
  • Washable electrostatic filters: rinse about monthly and let them dry fully.

Change them more often during smoke events, remodeling, or if you have several pets. When you replace a filter, match the size printed on the frame and point the airflow arrow toward the furnace or air handler.
faqs: Where is my HVAC filter located?

Most homes have the filter in the return grille, often in a hallway ceiling or wall. Others keep it in a slot at the furnace or air handler, which may be in the attic, garage or a closet. Some homes have filters in more than one place.
Why does my filter size say one thing but measure smaller?
The printed size is a nominal size, rounded up for easy shopping. The actual filter is usually a little smaller so it fits the slot. Buy by the size printed on your current filter.
Can I use a HEPA filter in my central air system?

Most residential systems aren't built for the airflow resistance of a true HEPA filter. If you want HEPA-level cleaning, a portable unit or a properly designed whole-home purifier is usually a better fit.
They can, since you don't buy replacements. The tradeoff is regular cleaning and drying. A washable filter put back in damp can grow mold, and many have lower filtration than a good pleated filter.
